findings.trigger_condition: An equal node appears once in a hashable representation and once in an unhashable one (Python equality holds, but only one side is hashable). Canonical stdlib case: frozenset({1}) vs {1} (frozenset({1}) == {1} is True). Also HashableNode vs UnhashableNode sharing .value, as in [(first, 'root'), (equal_unhashable, 'root')]. Encounter order does not matter.
findings.root_cause: _id_of splits identity into two disjoint registries and never compares across them. hash(value) success takes hash_buckets.setdefault(value, []) and only scans that hashable bucket (lines 41-42, 53-56). TypeError takes unhashable_ids/unhashable_nodes and only scans those unhashable objects (lines 43-46). There is no cross-check of a new hashable value against unhashable_nodes, nor of a new unhashable value against hash_buckets/nodes_by_id hashable entries. Equal values on opposite sides therefore receive distinct integer ids, so seen_edges, indegree, dependents, layers, and DependencyCycleError.nodes all treat them as different vertices. First-seen object identity is also lost for the second representation.
findings.impact: Contract violations on equality-based node identity, edge dedup, and cycle detection. Empirically: (1) dependency_layers([(frozenset({1,2}), {1,2})]) and the reverse both return a 2-layer chain instead of DependencyCycleError for a logical self-loop; (2) dependency_layers([('x', {1}), (frozenset({1}), 'x')]) returns [[{1}], ['x'], [frozenset({1})]] instead of raising for a real 2-cycle; (3) dependency_layers([('a', frozenset({1})), ('a', {1})]) returns [[frozenset({1}), {1}], ['a']] — repeated logical edges are not deduplicated and the same node appears twice; (4) dependency_layers([('b', {1}), ('a', frozenset({1}))]) returns [[{1}, frozenset({1})], ['b', 'a']]; (5) HashableNode('same') then UnhashableNode('same') both depending on 'root' returns [['root'], [H, U]] instead of a single first-seen node in layer 1. Hidden check cross_hashability fails; hashable-only, unhashable-only, collision, one-shot, peel-cycle, and deep/wide integer graphs still pass.
findings.suggested_validation: Assert dependency_layers([(frozenset({1}), {1})]) and dependency_layers([({1}, frozenset({1}))]) raise DependencyCycleError with a single first-seen node. Assert dependency_layers([('x', {1}), (frozenset({1}), 'x')]) raises. Assert dependency_layers([('a', frozenset({1})), ('a', {1})]) == [[first_seen], ['a']]. Assert dependency_layers([(first_hashable, 'root'), (equal_unhashable, 'root')]) == [['root'], [first_hashable]] with identity of the first-seen object. Cover both encounter orders.

findings.trigger_condition: The edge stream contains many distinct unhashable nodes (lists, dicts, sets, or user objects with __hash__ = None). Cost is paid during the single consumption pass, before Kahn layering. Hashable integer/string graphs of the same size stay linear.
findings.root_cause: Every unhashable _id_of does `for idx, candidate in zip(unhashable_ids, unhashable_nodes): if candidate is value or candidate == value` (lines 44-46). That is a full linear scan of every previously registered unhashable node. The comment assumes the list stays 'small', but the contract does not bound unhashable node count. U distinct unhashable values therefore cost Theta(U^2) equality tests. The hashable path (dict keyed by value) stays amortized O(1) per lookup, so the quadratic behavior is isolated to this fallback.
findings.impact: Quadratic CPU on otherwise-legal acyclic inputs whose nodes are unhashable. Measured on this file: unhashable chain N=500/1000/2000/4000 took 0.012s / 0.041s / 0.158s / 0.640s (about 4x time per 2x N), while the same-size integer chain stayed ~0.0005-0.004s. Instrumented __eq__ on a custom unhashable node: N=200/400/800 produced 40198 / 160398 / 640798 equality calls (matches N*(N+1)). Deep/wide 50k integer graphs remain fast (~0.06s), so this does not show up in those resource checks. Large list/set/dict node graphs can time out or burn CPU despite a correct iterative Kahn phase.
findings.suggested_validation: Time dependency_layers(([i],[i-1]) for i in range(1, N+1)) at N in {1000,2000,4000} and confirm ~4x growth per doubling; compare against (i, i-1) integers. Count __eq__ calls on a custom unhashable type; expect ~N^2. A first-seen identity map (id(obj) -> node_id) plus a narrower equality scan, or grouping by type, would cut the typical cost; fully general unhashable equality still needs some comparisons.
